instructions: Fill a large pot with water and put it on to boil for the noodles.
Scrub the mussels and pull off the beards. Cut the squid into 1-inch pieces. Pat the shrimp dry.
Slice the onion, cut the carrot and zucchini into matchsticks, cut the cabbage into 2-inch pieces and slice the shiitake. Cut the scallions into 2-inch lengths, mince the ginger and mince the garlic.
Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium-high. Add the onion, carrot, cabbage, zucchini, shiitake, the scallions and the salt. Cook for 3 minutes, stirring, until the cabbage starts to wilt.
Add the ginger, garlic and 2 tbsp of the gochugaru. Stir for 30 seconds, until it smells fragrant. Don't let it scorch.
Add the broth, 4 cups of water and the soy sauce. Bring it to a boil and simmer for 4 minutes.
While the soup simmers, boil the udon in the pot of water for the time on the package, usually 2 to 3 minutes. Drain and divide it among 4 bowls.

Add the mussels to the soup, cover, and cook for 2 minutes. Add the shrimp and squid and cook for 3 minutes, until the mussel shells open, the shrimp are pink and curled, and the squid is white all the way through. Throw away any mussels that stay shut.
Season with the pepper. Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Ladle the soup and seafood over the noodles. Put the remaining 1 tbsp gochugaru in a small bowl for the adults to stir in at the table.
method_notes: Korean Bapsang is the lead (4.54 from 65 ratings): vegetables stir-fried with ginger, scallion and gochugaru, then stock, then clams, mussels, shrimp and squid, ladled over noodles. Two Plaid Aprons and Beyond Kimchee agree on a gochugaru-red broth, vegetables first and seafood last, and noodles cooked separately. The lead includes pork and clams; here the pork is dropped (Beyond Kimchee lists it as optional) and clams are skipped to keep the shopping and the time down. Only 2 tbsp of gochugaru goes in the pot, and the rest goes on the table, to keep the base mild. Honest time is just over 30 minutes.
